source: Tversky & Kahneman (1981) The framing of decisions and the psychology of choice, Science 211:453-458
finding: Founding Asian disease experiment. Same cover story (600 expected deaths), same outcomes; only the wording changes between gains (saved) and losses (die). The sure option wins in the gain wording and loses in the loss wording.
numbers: Problem 1 (gain wording) N=152: Program A, 200 saved for sure, 72%; Program B, 1/3 chance 600 saved and 2/3 chance none saved, 28%. Problem 2 (loss wording) N=155: Program C, 400 die for sure, 22%; Program D, 1/3 chance nobody dies and 2/3 chance 600 die, 78%. Between-subjects.
limits: Between-subjects. Hypothetical. The paper says the reversal was seen in several groups including university faculty and physicians (no group numbers given).
agent_relevance: Two wordings of one problem can flip the answer. Our S1 second-wording check tests exactly this flip.

source: Tversky & Kahneman (1981) The framing of decisions and the psychology of choice, Science 211:453-458
finding: The authors explain the reversal with an S-shaped value function plus the framing of outcomes as gains or losses from a reference point. Value is concave above the reference point, convex below it, and steeper for losses.
numbers: Problems 1 and 2 are called 'effectively identical'; the shift is from risk aversion (72% sure) to risk taking (78% gamble). The paper says the effects are 'large and systematic, although by no means universal' and are 'not eliminated by monetary incentives'.
limits: Value function is given qualitatively (Fig. 1 is hypothetical). No parameters are fitted in this paper.
agent_relevance: The effect comes from the reference point the wording sets. A neutral restatement in final states removes that cue.

source: Tversky & Kahneman (1981) The framing of decisions and the psychology of choice, Science 211:453-458
finding: Concurrent decisions: people fail to integrate two choices, treat each in its own frame, and end up with a dominated combination.
numbers: Problem 3 N=150: decision (i) sure gain $240 chosen by 84% vs 25% chance of $1000 16%. Decision (ii) sure loss $750 chosen by 13% vs 75% chance to lose $1000 87%. Combination A and D chosen by 73%; dominant B and C by only 3%. Problem 4 N=86, the combinations shown side by side: B and C 100%, A and D 0%.
limits: Hypothetical in the main run.
agent_relevance: When two sub-questions come together, the agent should merge them into one final-outcome table before choosing.

source: Tversky & Kahneman (1981) The framing of decisions and the psychology of choice, Science 211:453-458
finding: Paid version: framing effects were not removed by real pay.
numbers: Footnote: N=126, outcomes cut by a factor of 50, one participant in ten paid by coin tosses. 67% chose A (sure gain) and 86% chose D (risky loss). The dominated combination A and D was chosen by 60%; the dominant combination only 6%.
limits: Small stakes; only one in ten paid.
agent_relevance: Stating that stakes are real is unlikely to fix a wording flip in a model either; test it.

source: Tversky & Kahneman (1981) The framing of decisions and the psychology of choice, Science 211:453-458
finding: Pseudocertainty effect: a two-stage story makes a risky gain look like a sure gain, so stage wording changes choice when final odds are identical.
numbers: Problem 5 N=77: sure $30 78%, 80% chance of $45 22%. Problem 6 N=85 (two-stage game, 25% chance to reach stage 2): sure $30 in stage 2 74%, 80% chance of $45 26%. Problem 7 N=81 (same final odds, direct): 25% chance of $30 42%, 20% chance of $45 58%. Problems 6 and 7 have identical outcomes and probabilities.
limits: Different groups per problem; small N.
agent_relevance: A multi-stage story can hide the shared branch. Final-outcome probabilities should be computed in code.

source: Tversky & Kahneman (1981) The framing of decisions and the psychology of choice, Science 211:453-458
finding: Mental accounting: the same $5 saving is judged inside different accounts, so choices depend on the price context.
numbers: Problem 10: willing to drive 20 minutes to save $5 on a calculator: 68% when it costs $15 (N=93), 29% when it costs $125 (N=88). Problem 8 N=183: buy a new $10 ticket after losing $10 cash, 88% yes. Problem 9 N=200: buy again after losing the ticket, 46% yes.
limits: Riskless framing, not risky choice. Hypothetical.
agent_relevance: Relative versus absolute framing of the same number is another variable a second wording should change.

source: Tversky & Kahneman (1981) The framing of decisions and the psychology of choice, Science 211:453-458
finding: Authors say people are usually unaware of alternative frames and often cannot settle the inconsistency even once they see it. Their analogy is a mountain that looks different from different vantage points.
numbers: They list four aspects: (i) another frame may flip preference, (ii) people are unaware of other frames, (iii) they want frame-independent preferences, (iv) they are unsure how to resolve conflicts. In Problems 3-4 and 8-9 one frame is clearly better once compared; in 1-2 and 6-7 it is not obvious which to give up.
limits: For Asian disease no single wording is correct, so the flip cannot be repaired by choosing the right frame.
agent_relevance: Direct support for a second-wording operator: detect the flip, then pick by a rule in code, not by the model's opinion.

source: Kahneman & Tversky (1979) Prospect theory: an analysis of decision under risk, Econometrica 47:263-291
finding: Original prospect theory data. Reflection effect: preferences among negative prospects mirror those among positive prospects. This is the empirical base of the 1981 gain-loss reversal.
limits: Hypothetical money gambles; majority patterns.
agent_relevance: Gain wording brings out risk aversion and loss wording risk seeking. Flipping the sign is a measurable test of a model.

source: Kahneman & Tversky (1979) Prospect theory: an analysis of decision under risk, Econometrica 47:263-291
finding: Certainty effect and the Allais violation: moving a probability away from certainty costs more than the same change between two uncertain values.
numbers: Problem 1 N=72: sure 2,400 chosen by 82% over (2,500,.33; 2,400,.66). Problem 2 N=72: (2,500,.33) chosen by 83% over (2,400,.34). 61% made the modal choice in both, which violates expected utility. Problem 3 N=95: 80% sure 3,000. Problem 5 N=72: sure tour 78%; Problem 6 N=72: 67% chose the 5% chance of the larger tour.
limits: Hypothetical. Majority patterns, not all individuals.
agent_relevance: Human data are not 'correct' answers. An agent that maximises expected value will look different from people and is right.

source: Kahneman & Tversky (1979) Prospect theory: an analysis of decision under risk, Econometrica 47:263-291
finding: Isolation effect and editing: people drop shared components and focus on what differs, so two decompositions of the same problem get different choices; bonuses are not integrated into final states.
numbers: Problem 10 (two-stage game) N=141: 78% chose the sure 3,000 over (4,000,.80) after a shared .75 chance of nothing, although Problem 4 (same final odds) gave 65% for (4,000,.20). Problems 11 and 12: with a 1,000 bonus 84% took the sure 500 (N=70); with a 2,000 bonus 69% took the gamble on losses (N=68); final states are identical.
limits: Hypothetical; separate groups per problem.
agent_relevance: Framing works through editing of the problem. The agent should write final-state outcomes before choosing.

source: Kahneman & Tversky (1979) Prospect theory: an analysis of decision under risk, Econometrica 47:263-291
finding: Formal model: overall value V = sum of pi(p_i) times v(x_i). v is defined on changes from a reference point, concave for gains, convex for losses, steeper for losses. pi is a decision weight, not a probability, with subcertainty and overweighting of small p.
numbers: Stated properties: pi(0)=0, pi(1)=1; pi(p)>p for small p; pi(p)+pi(1-p)<1; subproportionality. Evidence: Problem 14 N=72, 72% prefer a .001 chance of 5,000 to sure 5; Problem 14' N=72, 83% prefer sure loss of 5 to a .001 chance of -5,000. Problem 13 N=68 (82%) and 13' N=64 (70%) support concave gains and convex losses.
limits: 1979 version has no fitted parameters and covers prospects with at most two nonzero outcomes. Two phases: editing, then evaluation.
agent_relevance: The formal reason a wording shift matters: wording sets the reference point, which defines gain and loss.

source: Tversky & Kahneman (1992) Advances in prospect theory: cumulative representation of uncertainty, J Risk Uncertainty 5:297-323 (parameter values read second-hand from the Wakker program page)
finding: Cumulative prospect theory median parameter estimates, as stated by a page that implements them.
numbers: alpha = 0.88 (gains power), beta = 0.88 (losses power), lambda = 2.25 (loss aversion), gamma = 0.61 (weighting, gains), delta = 0.69 (weighting, losses). Another source quoted delta = 0.65; Tarabeih (2026) quotes the original weighting as 0.65.
limits: I could not open the 1992 PDF. Values read from the calculator page, which cites T&K. Medians; individual variation is large.
agent_relevance: Gives numbers for a simulated human-like agent and a yardstick for LLM fits.

source: Wikipedia: Framing effect (psychology)
finding: Summary page confirms the headline figures and lists moderators.
numbers: Positive frame 72% chose Treatment A (saves 200 of 600); negative frame 78% chose the risky treatment (33% chance all saved, 66% none). Older adults more susceptible, mainly to negative frames. Effect 'seems to diminish in a non-native language'. Reduced or removed with ample credible information.
limits: Encyclopedia; no sample sizes; 33%/66% are roundings of 1/3 and 2/3.
agent_relevance: Moderator list for later angles: language, age, credible information.

source: Kahneman (2003; Nobel lecture 2002) Maps of bounded rationality: psychology for behavioral economics
finding: Kahneman's later account: framing works through accessibility. Different wordings make different attributes salient, and people passively accept the formulation they are given.
numbers: On the certain option: 'the certainty of saving people is disproportionately attractive, and the certainty of deaths is disproportionately aversive.' People who compare both versions 'almost always conclude that the same action should be taken in both'.
quote: Passive adoption of the formulation given appears to be a general principle
limits: Review by an original author; no new sample sizes for Asian disease.
agent_relevance: The frames are effectively identical on reflection, so an agent can detect the flip by reading both wordings together.

source: Kahneman (2003; Nobel lecture 2002) Maps of bounded rationality: psychology for behavioral economics
finding: Definition: framing effects are restricted to discrepancies between problems that decision makers, on reflection, consider effectively identical. Invariance (Tversky and Kahneman 1986) or extensionality (Arrow 1982) is the broken assumption.
numbers: McNeil, Pauker, Sox, Tversky (1982): surgery versus radiation described by survival rate or mortality rate. 90% short-term survival is less threatening than 10% immediate mortality, so the survival frame gave a substantially higher preference for surgery, 'no less pronounced among experienced physicians than among patients'. The lecture gives no percentages.
limits: McNeil figures not read; lecture only summarises them.
agent_relevance: Expert knowledge does not protect against wording; a strong model may not be protected either.

source: Kahneman (2003; Nobel lecture 2002) Maps of bounded rationality: psychology for behavioral economics
finding: Thoughtfulness helps only when both versions are seen. LeBoeuf and Shafir (large study) did not replicate the earlier claim (Smith and Levin 1996) that need for cognition reduces framing between subjects; LeBoeuf and Shafir (2003) found more thoughtful people are more consistent within subject.
numbers: Quote: 'Thoughtfulness confers no advantage in the absence of a relevant cue.' No sample numbers in the lecture.
limits: Secondary description; numbers not given.
agent_relevance: Thinking harder in one pass will not fix a flip. The cue is the second wording. Supports G1: doubt on a signal, here disagreement between wordings.

source: Kahneman (2003; Nobel lecture 2002) Maps of bounded rationality: psychology for behavioral economics
finding: Framing beyond choice. Simon and Hayes (1976) found Tower of Hanoi isomorphs varied greatly in difficulty; Shafir (1993) found a richly described custody parent was favoured under both 'accept' and 'reject' instructions.
numbers: Simon and Hayes: subjects 'will adopt the representation that constitutes the most straightforward translation'. No difficulty percentages in the lecture.
limits: Hanoi and custody numbers not given.
agent_relevance: Wording sensitivity also appears in problem solving. The second-wording operator is not only for gambles.

source: Kahneman (2003; Nobel lecture 2002) Maps of bounded rationality: psychology for behavioral economics
finding: Wealth versus change formulation: people do not compute final wealth from the stated gains and losses. Problem 4 (own W, or 50% W-100 and 50% W+150) gives a mild preference for the gamble; the gain-loss twin gives risk aversion. This is a framing effect by the definition.
numbers: Qualitative: 'informal experiments... have consistently yielded a mild preference for the uncertain state of wealth'. No N.
limits: Informal data, no counts.
agent_relevance: Restating a problem as final states is a concrete cleaning step.

source: Reyna & Brainerd (2011) Dual processes in decision making and developmental neuroscience: a fuzzy-trace model, Developmental Review
finding: Fuzzy-trace theory: people keep gist (some versus none) and verbatim numbers. Gain wording gist is 'some saved for sure' versus 'some saved or none'; loss wording gist is 'some die' versus 'some die or none die', and people prefer the gamble.
numbers: Numbers-deleted test (Reyna and Brainerd 1991): every non-zero number replaced by 'some'. Framing was largest when all numbers were removed: 90% chose the sure option in the gain frame and 86% chose the gamble in the loss frame. Replicated for lives and money, and over eight blocks (framing grew with blocks).
limits: Described in a review by the theory's authors; per-group N not shown.
agent_relevance: Numbers are not needed for the flip. The some-versus-none contrast may be what a language model reacts to.

source: Reyna & Brainerd (2011) Dual processes in decision making and developmental neuroscience: a fuzzy-trace model, Developmental Review
finding: Critical test of prospect theory against fuzzy-trace theory: moving the zero complement out of focus removes framing; removing numbers while keeping the some-versus-none contrast keeps it.
numbers: Truncated gamble (only '1/3 probability that 600 will be saved', zero complement in the preamble): framing effects disappeared. The opposite truncation produced large framing effects. When told the choice would be repeated many times, framing declined or disappeared (Keren 1991).
limits: Review text; no per-condition N. Proponent authors.
agent_relevance: A prompt that hides the zero complement may remove the flip; one that keeps only some versus none may deepen it. Both are testable on a model.

source: Reyna & Brainerd (2011) Dual processes in decision making and developmental neuroscience: a fuzzy-trace model, Developmental Review
finding: Developmental and individual difference claims: framing emerges in early adolescence as gist-based intuition develops; autistic people, who lean on verbatim analysis, show smaller framing bias; experts use fewer risk dimensions and more all-or-none decisions.
numbers: Abstract: framing effects 'emerge in early adolescence'; 'In autistic individuals... framing biases are attenuated.' No effect sizes in the text read.
limits: Review. Derivation of prospect theory from fuzzy-trace theory is theoretical.
agent_relevance: Against the idea that more careful analysis always helps: in this theory advanced reasoning is more gist-based.

source: Pinon & Gambara (2005) A meta-analytic review of framing effect: risky, attribute and goal framing, Psicothema 17:325-331
finding: Meta-analysis of 51 studies (1997 to 2003), 151 effect sizes, about 13,500 subjects. Risky framing d = 0.437, attribute d = 0.260, goal d = 0.444.
numbers: Risky framing larger with more women and with a single risky option; most frequent task was the Asian disease problem; student samples 83.4% of studies; the regression for risky framing explained R2 = 0.290.
limits: Only 1997 to 2003. Published studies; no bias correction.
agent_relevance: Typical effect is moderate (d about 0.4), not a full reversal. Expect partial shifts when measuring a model.

source: Kuhberger (1998) The influence of framing on risky decisions: a meta-analysis, OBHDP 75:23-55 (figures from a search summary)
finding: Earlier meta-analysis: 230 effect sizes from 136 studies, mean framing effect d = 0.31.
numbers: A later p-curve reanalysis (Steiger and Kuhberger) is reported to give a corrected d = 0.52. Figures come from a search summary, not the paper.
limits: Not opened. Unverified.
agent_relevance: A moderate pooled effect whose size depends on the correction method.

source: Klein et al. (2014) Investigating variation in replicability: Many Labs replication project, Social Psychology (figures from search summaries)
finding: Many Labs 1 replicated the Asian disease gain-loss framing across 36 samples; effect smaller than the original.
numbers: A review says replication effect was 53% to 67% of the original size (99% CI). A replication atlas entry reports chi2(1)=516.41, d=0.60. A blog says 31 of 36 labs were significant; unverified.
limits: Not opened (download failed). All figures second-hand.
agent_relevance: The core effect replicates in large samples. Model tests should use many wordings and runs.

source: Zhou, Liu, Liao, Li (2021) Risky choice framing with various problem descriptions: a replication and extension study, Judgment and Decision Making 16:394-421 (from search summary)
finding: Direct replication of Kuhberger and Tanner (2010) with a Chinese sample. Type 1 task (classic) gave a framing effect, Type 2 (zero complement of the risky option removed) none, Type 3 a large one. Supports fuzzy-trace theory over prospect theory.
numbers: Extension varied probability and expected-value ratios. Numbers not read.
limits: Not opened; secondary summary only.
agent_relevance: Which part of the wording carries the effect: the zero complement of the gamble.

source: Mandel (2001) Gain-loss framing and choice: separating outcome formulations from descriptor formulations, OBHDP 85:56-76 (secondary mention only)
finding: A later paper lists Mandel (2001) with Fagley and Miller (1987) and Takemura (1992, 1993) among studies where the classic phenomenon did not fully replicate.
numbers: Numbers not read.
limits: Not opened; only a citation list seen.
agent_relevance: Failed or partial replications depend on exact descriptor wording (for example 'at least' versus exactly). Fine print matters.

source: Tarabeih (2026) Prospect theory in large language models: a meta-analysis of loss aversion, diminishing sensitivity and probability weighting (arXiv 2610.33103)
finding: Meta-analysis of prospect-theory parameters fitted to LLMs: 102 estimates, 11 studies, 32 models. LLMs show low loss aversion, near-linear value under one method, human-like probability weighting.
numbers: Pooled lambda = 1.26 (95% CI 1.06 to 1.46) vs human 1.96, 1.31 or 1.07 in three meta-analyses. Symmetric designs: 1.15 vs 1.07 human; losses smaller than gains: 1.46 vs 2.3. Curvature 1.01 (Tversky-Kahneman method) vs human 0.67; 0.52 under Tanaka method. Weighting 0.81 (T&K) and 0.84 (Tanaka). Model families differ widely.
limits: Few studies for weighting (4) and curvature (6). Imputed standard errors. Parameter fits do not test framing directly.
agent_relevance: Models show weak loss aversion on described gambles, so a framing flip in a model probably comes from wording cues more than from the human value function.

source: Wang et al. (2025, v5 2026) Rethinking prospect theory for LLMs: revealing the instability of decision-making under epistemic uncertainty (arXiv 2508.08992)
finding: Prospect theory does not describe every LLM. Fit judged by MAE and McFadden pseudo-R2; Llama-3.1-8B and Qwen2.5-14B fail the criteria (MAE above 0.20, pseudo-R2 below 0.10).
numbers: Among reliable fits the risk parameter mostly lies between 0.4 and 0.6; loss aversion is unstable (some models above 1, some below 1; boundary values for Llama-3.1-8B and Qwen2.5-7B). Replacing numeric probabilities with verbal markers mapped to the same probability changed choices and fitted parameters.
limits: Tanaka price lists, not the Asian disease frame.
agent_relevance: Verbal versus numeric wording of probability alone moves LLM choices; use numeric canonical forms.

source: Zhang et al. (2026) Same probabilities, different advice: gain-loss framing effects in high-stakes LLM decision support (arXiv 2610.29294, FrameBench-HPS)
finding: 2,880 prompts from 240 high-stakes scenarios (health, finance, education and career, legal) test gain versus loss wording of the same probability on seven LLMs.
numbers: Recommendation category changed in 32.41% of 6,644 complete groups (95% CI 30.48 to 34.36); direct yes-no reversals 0.63%; 98.1% of 2,153 changes involve the 'uncertain' category. Probability canonicalization (state both complementary probabilities) cut the loss-minus-gain risk shift from 0.363 to -0.010; frame-robust prompting left a 22.83% category-change rate, an 11.37-point cut.
limits: No human arm; mitigation tested on 3 models and 32 held-out scenarios. Preprint.
agent_relevance: Best direct support for S1: restate both complementary probabilities in code; it beats an instruction to ignore the frame.

source: Wang & Zhang (2026) Framing effects in independent-agent LLMs: a cross-family behavioral analysis (arXiv 2603.19282)
finding: Two logically equivalent framings of a threshold voting task across 82 models in 11 families, 20 independent trials per prompt. Wording alone dominated the choice distribution.
numbers: Instrumental framing: option B in 4.3% of trials. Cooperative framing: option B in 68.8% of trials. Susceptibility differed significantly between lineages.
limits: Not a gain-loss Asian disease frame. Preprint.
agent_relevance: Framing swings in models can be larger than the 1981 human swing; test our own model per task.

source: Lim, Kim, Whang (2026) DeFrame: debiasing LLMs against framing effects (arXiv 2602.04306)
finding: Fairness scores change with the framing of the same question ('A is better than B' vs 'B is worse than A'). Existing debiasing improves frame-averaged fairness but may not reduce framing disparity, sometimes raising it.
numbers: Across 8 LLMs, DeFrame lowers framing disparity by 92% and bias score by 93% on average on BBQ (authors' claim from the abstract).
limits: Fairness benchmarks, not gain-loss risky choice. Author-reported averages.
agent_relevance: Asking the same item in several frames and checking consistency is a known mitigation direction.
